REVIEW:
# Review: Evening and Saturday Hours Memo

The memo is clear and well structured, and its arithmetic for the full pilot checks out. The main problems are in the proposed smaller test. Its cost and staffing numbers don't match each other, and it rests on a misreading of the staff survey. Because the director will act on the test, those issues matter most.

## Arithmetic check

| Claim | Check | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 28 h × $310 = $8,680/week | ✓ | Correct |
| $340 × 60% = $204 | ✓ | Correct |
| ~43 visits/week, 1.5/hour | 8,680 ÷ 204 = 42.5 | Correct |
| ~550 visits/month across 3 clinics | 42.5 × 3 × 4.33 ≈ 552 | Correct |
| ~three-quarters of 730 treatable calls | 552 ÷ 730 ≈ 76% | Correct |
| ~$1.35M/year | 8,680 × 3 × 52 = $1,354,080 | Correct |
| 84 vet-hours, about two full-time vets | 28 × 3 | Correct |
| Saturday ~$2,500/week, ~$130K/year | 8 × 310 = $2,480 | Correct, but see issue 1 |
| ~12 visits per Saturday to break even | 2,480 ÷ 204 = 12.2 | Correct, but see issue 1 |
| "About a tenth of the cost" | 130K ÷ 1.35M ≈ 9.6% | Correct |

## Major issues (fix before sending)

**1. The Saturday cost leaves out the premium the memo itself says will be paid.**
The staffing bullet says vets will be "paid at a premium." But the $2,500 cost and the 12-visit break-even use the base $310 rate. The memo also criticises the full pilot for ignoring the premium, so this inconsistency is easy to spot.
- A 20–25% premium on the vet's share of $310 raises break-even to roughly 13–14 visits.
- That leaves the 15-visit expansion trigger only slightly above break-even.
- The fix is to show the premium-adjusted figure and reconsider the trigger.

**2. The "roughly 30% of vets willing to work extra hours" figure is not in the brief.**
The survey found that 70% would not work *regular evening shifts*. That does not mean 30% would work Saturdays or extra hours. Some of the 70% might accept Saturdays, and some of the 30% might not. The test's staffing plan ("no new hires needed") depends on this misreading.

There is also a second problem. With 4 vet positions already unfilled, current vets are probably stretched. Adding Saturday shifts risks burnout and daytime gaps, which is the same objection the memo raises against the full pilot.

**3. "Protects the Valley relationship" is asserted, not shown.**
The Saturday test still competes for urgent cases, which is exactly what Valley's owner objected to. The planned meeting may help, but the memo presents a hoped-for outcome as a benefit. A safer wording would be "reduces the risk to," along with what happens if she reacts anyway.

**4. The memo never explains why the small test is feasible.**
The case against the full pilot is that it needs too many visits. The Saturday test needs the same rate, about 1.5 visits per open hour. What differs is the total: about 52 visits a month, or roughly 7% of treatable after-hours calls, compared with about 76% for the full pilot. Stating that comparison directly is the strongest argument for the recommendation, and it is currently missing.

## Moderate issues

- **Unused brief data that would help the case.**
  - Valley's $890 average invoice against Brookside's $340 is a large price advantage. It makes the 72% preference figure more believable.
  - The 25-minute drive to Valley is a convenience argument for opening locally.
- **"Many of those calls come overnight, on Sundays or on holidays."** There is no data for this. The memo's own action list (logging calls by hour and day) admits the data don't exist yet. It should be framed as an assumption.
- **Cannibalisation isn't discussed.** Some Saturday visits would otherwise have been Monday daytime visits. Those aren't new contribution.
- **The data-collection timing doesn't fit the decision.** Logging calls "before the end of the month" won't produce useful data before the director's end-of-month deadline. Make it an ongoing step that informs the choice of clinic and the launch.
- **The northern-suburbs reasoning runs the wrong way.** The brief says the client base is concentrated in the north. The memo instead infers client location from the number of clinics there. Cite the client concentration directly.
- **"Giving up this market permanently" is overstated.** "Risk losing ground to an established competitor" is closer to what the evidence supports.

## Your expected-issues list

I agree with all ten points, with these notes:
- **#3 (premium not quantified)** matters more for the Saturday test than for the full pilot. See issue 1.
- **#10 (staffing untested)** understates the problem. The 30% figure is a misreading, not just untested. See issue 2.
- **#5 (ramp-up) and #6 (Saturday not representative)** point to the same fix: define what a "fail" at 3 months means, and whether evening demand will be tested separately.
- **#9 (alternatives)** is partly covered. The memo raises a Valley partnership as an option for the meeting but doesn't assess it as an alternative to the pilot.

**Additions to your list:** issues 1–4 above, cannibalisation, the unused $890 and 25-minute data, and the formatting items below.

## Formatting and length

- There is a stray `---` followed by an empty `##` heading at the end. Remove both.
- `[Analyst]` is still a placeholder.
- Length is at or slightly over the 550-word upper limit. Fixing the issues above will add words, so cut elsewhere. "Why not do nothing" and the closing paragraph could both be shorter.
